messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Bartender
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Worst Case Rehearsal: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared, Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Nadia is a 30-year-old Middle Eastern American woman who came to treatment after years of trying to live inside a world she experiences as narrow and precarious. She grew up in a home where violence between her parents could erupt without warning. Her clearest sensory impressions are not a tidy story but flashes: her father’s arm moving too fast, a chair scraping hard across the floor, her mother’s breath turning ragged, the slam of a door, the metallic click of locks afterward. As a child she would freeze and listen from the hallway, straining to tell from movement and sound whether the danger was about to get worse. Even now, when she tries to describe what she witnessed, she says she knows exactly what happened but cannot find words for it. If she pushes herself to talk, she becomes so flooded that she has to stop.

Those early experiences left Nadia with a settled conviction that people are not to be trusted, and that she cannot rely on herself to do the right thing in a crisis. She has come to believe that when something turns dangerous, she will misread it or freeze, just as she feels she did as a child. That sense of mistrust and self-doubt keeps her body on alert. Sudden movements by other people, especially a quick reach across a room or a sharp turn of the shoulders, put her immediately on guard before she has time to think. She feels safe only in a very small number of places, mainly her apartment and one back storage area at work where she can see the door. At night she repeatedly checks the locks and windows, not once but over and over, because she does not trust either other people or her own first judgment that things are secure.

Her work as a bartender brings these fears into daily life. In the bar, when customers stand abruptly, swing an arm while talking, or move behind the counter unexpectedly, Nadia’s whole body tightens. She scans exits and tracks where everyone is standing. Open spaces are particularly hard for her; being out on the floor during a busy shift, exposed from several directions, feels intolerably vulnerable, and she finds reasons to stay near enclosed corners or behind the bar. Because she feels under threat so easily, she tries to manage it by mentally rehearsing worst-case scenarios—what she would do if a customer became violent, if someone came through the door angry, if she had to escape through the back. She also works hard to control her emotions, believing that if she lets herself feel fear or panic, she will lose control completely.

These efforts are meant to keep her safe, but they also keep the trauma close. When Nadia rehearses disaster in her head, the old scenes come back not as a coherent account but as bodily fragments and overpowering emotion. A customer’s sudden movement at work can pull up an image of her father’s arm or the sound of impact before she has words for what she is remembering. Because the memory arrives in this raw, nonverbal way, it feels immediate and dangerous, which only confirms for her that the threat is still everywhere. She has noticed that after a shift when she has been especially watchful, the memories are harder to hold onto long enough to explain; she goes blank, overwhelmed, and ashamed of not being able to say something so central to her own life.

Over time, the ways Nadia copes have deepened her doubts about herself. She interprets the fact that she must rehearse every possible catastrophe as proof that she cannot rely on herself naturally. Her strict effort to control emotion feels, in her mind, like evidence that she is only barely holding together. Avoiding open spaces has made her life smaller; she turns down invitations, leaves crowded places early, and chooses routes home that keep her near buildings and away from exposed stretches. At work, coworkers have noticed she is most comfortable in restricted parts of the bar and can seem distant when the room gets busy. Nadia reads this as further confirmation that she cannot trust herself around people and cannot trust them either.

The memories also feed that same conclusion. Each time she cannot put the childhood violence into words, she feels defective and uncertain, as though not being able to narrate it means she never really understood what was happening and still would not know what to do now. And because the memories are so overwhelming when they surface, she becomes even more vigilant for signs of danger, more certain that safety exists only in a few tightly controlled places. By the time she sought help, she was exhausted from living this way—checking locks repeatedly, bracing at sudden movements, silently playing out disasters before every shift. What finally brought her in was the fear that her world was shrinking to just a few safe zones, and the hope, still tentative, that she might learn how to remember what happened without being swallowed by it and without feeling that danger is waiting in every movement around her.
